subject: || does not propagate lvalue context to its operands: for (pos $x || pos $y) { $_++ } writes nothing (op/or.t t9/t10)
description:
DIAGNOSED s319 (probe s319/pr-or.pl).

  my ($x,$y); $y = " ";
  for (pos $x || pos $y) { eval { $_++ } }
  perl: pos($y) == 1        PCL: pos($y) is undef/""     <-- t9 (rhs)

  $x = "  "; pos $x = 1;
  for (pos $x || pos $y) { eval { $_++ } }
  perl: pos($x) == 2        PCL: pos($x) stays 1         <-- t10 (lhs)

So the foreach alias `$_` is bound to a COPY of whichever operand `||` selected,
and `$_++` writes into that copy.  perl propagates lvalue-ish context through
`||` to BOTH operands, so the alias is the real `pos` magic cell and the
increment lands on it.

TWO features are stacked here, and BOTH are needed for these rows:
 1. lvalue-context propagation through `||` (and by symmetry `&&`, `//`) to the
    operand that is actually returned;
 2. `pos` as an lvalue/magic cell that an alias can write through
    (see reference_box_magic_hook — the same box-magic mechanism as $. / \substr
    / \vec; `pos $x = 1` already works, so the cell exists).

NOTE the sibling rows PASS: op/or.t t11/t12 assert that `||` does NOT propagate
lvalue context to a SUBSCRIPT on either side (`for ($h{k} || $h{l}) {}` must not
autovivify).  So any fix must propagate to a magic cell without autovivifying a
subscript — that asymmetry is the whole design constraint, and it is why a
blanket "make || an lvalue" change would break t11/t12.

perl itself is 13/1 on this file (one row is already not-ok for perl), so the
target is PCL 13/1, not 14/0.

SCOREBOARD: op/or.t 11/3 vs perl 13/1.  NOT registered as XDIFF: a fix target,
and not fully explained by any blessed section.
